A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents for worsening symptoms of previously diagnosed acute sinusitis. Initially, the pediatrician prescribed decongestants and sent the patient home. Since then, the patient has developed a nasal discharge with worsening pain. The patient has a medical history of asthma which is well-controlled with albuterol. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 90/48 mmHg, pulse is 124/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. Inspection of the patient's nose reveals a unilateral purulent discharge mixed with blood. The rest of the patient's exam is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Bleeding and infected vessel of Kiesselbach plexus
B. Foreign body obstruction
C. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
D. Septal perforation
E. Sinusitis with bacterial superinfection

knowledge_chunks.text: Both adult and child migraineurs are frequently misdiagnosed as having “sinus headaches”. In one adult study, 35% of the migraineurs had undergone previous sinus surgery. This was demonstrated by an observational study that included 3000 individuals with a history of self- or clinician-diagnosed “sinus headaches”, in which 88% of these patients met the diagnostic criteria for migraine. However, most of these patients reported additional typical migraine symptoms, such as photophobia, phonophobia, and pulsating head pain. Migraine can be mistaken for sinus headache because of the similarity in location of the headache and the commonly accompanying nasal autonomic symptoms. Pain due to pathology of the nasal mucosa or related structures is usually perceived as frontal or facial, but may be referred more posteriorly, making a proper diagnosis difficult. The presence of purulent nasal discharge and the character of the pain, which is typically pressure-like and reproduced by palpation over the sinuses, help to differentiate these two conditions.

As respiratory pediatricians we all experienced that low-dose inhaled corticosteroids can easily control asthma symptoms in most of patients. Moreover, exacerbations in children are often concentrated in some periods of the year due to viral trigger or aeroallergens, and some little patients can even stop their treatment in summer time without clinical deterioration. Nevertheless, children and their parents sometimes keep complaining of recurrent respiratory symptoms despite the correct and continuous treatment, and various courses of antibiotics, beta-2 agonists and oral corticosteroids are frequently prescribed by pediatrician. As a consequence of the poor symptoms control, asthma treatment is often increased and the patient categorized as “problematic severe asthmatic.” However, an earlier step could be identified and this condition better defined as “problematic respiratory symptoms unresponsive to prescribed asthma therapy”. In fact, the known expression: “Not all that wheezes is asthma” continues to be relevant and the asthma diagnosis should be clinically reconsidered. A hair visible in the skin ostium is considered to be pathognomonic for ND (Figure 1). NDs may be noticeable at birth, presenting as a lump or a pit on the nasal dorsum. The majority of them are diagnosed at infancy or in early childhood, but there are some reports of later diagnoses. A slow-growing mass may be observed in some cases in early infancy. Half of children may present hypertelorism and a broadened nasal bridge. Palpation may reveal a subcutaneous mass in 30% of patients, typically at the level of the osteocartilaginuous junction. Some authors have reported intracranial epidermoid and dermoid cysts in the proximity of the crista galli or foramen caecum without typical nasal manifestation. Intermittent sebaceous discharge from the skin ostium may be observed. Multiple ostia and cysts at more than one level are a rarity. Recurring infections influence the long-term results of surgical treatment. Presentation: A 29-year-old woman experienced recurrent bilateral purulent nasal discharge for 3 months. The symptoms began 3 months prior, accompanied by dizziness and headache. She had a cesarean birth at a local hospital 4 years ago and has no relevant family history. Physical examination revealed slightly congested mucosa in the bilateral nasal cavity, slightly enlarged inferior turbinates, hypertrophic middle turbinates, and a small amount of purulent nasal discharge in both middle nasal passages and posterior nostrils. Laboratory tests indicated slightly elevated serum uric acid (428.9 μmol/L), fibrin (4.9 g/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (30 mm/h), and ultrasensitive thyroid stimulating hormone (5.1 μIU/mL) levels, while myoglobin (< 21 ng/mL) was slightly decreased. Complete blood count, electrolyte profiles, and liver function were normal. A computed tomography scan from another hospital showed bilateral maxillary sinusitis, ethmoiditis, and bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy. A preoperative noncontrast chest computed tomography scan revealed a high-riding, tortuous structure extending to the mid-upper level of the first thoracic vertebra with local cystic dilatation, and a fe. Confirmed diagnosis: Cervical aortic arch with aneurysm formation and an anomalous right subclavian artery and left vertebral artery. Differential diagnosis includes: Cervical aortic arch with aneurysm formation and an anomalous right subclavian artery and left vertebral artery.

knowledge_chunks.text: Both adult and child migraineurs are frequently misdiagnosed as having “sinus headaches”. In one adult study, 35% of the migraineurs had undergone previous sinus surgery. This was demonstrated by an observational study that included 3000 individuals with a history of self- or clinician-diagnosed “sinus headaches”, in which 88% of these patients met the diagnostic criteria for migraine. However, most of these patients reported additional typical migraine symptoms, such as photophobia, phonophobia, and pulsating head pain. Migraine can be mistaken for sinus headache because of the similarity in location of the headache and the commonly accompanying nasal autonomic symptoms. Pain due to pathology of the nasal mucosa or related structures is usually perceived as frontal or facial, but may be referred more posteriorly, making a proper diagnosis difficult. The presence of purulent nasal discharge and the character of the pain, which is typically pressure-like and reproduced by palpation over the sinuses, help to differentiate these two conditions.

Moreover, exacerbations in children are often concentrated in some periods of the year due to viral trigger or aeroallergens, and some little patients can even stop their treatment in summer time without clinical deterioration. Nevertheless, children and their parents sometimes keep complaining of recurrent respiratory symptoms despite the correct and continuous treatment, and various courses of antibiotics, beta-2 agonists and oral corticosteroids are frequently prescribed by pediatrician. Presentation: A 29-year-old woman experienced recurrent bilateral purulent nasal discharge for 3 months. The symptoms began 3 months prior, accompanied by dizziness and headache. She had a cesarean birth at a local hospital 4 years ago and has no relevant family history. Physical examination revealed slightly congested mucosa in the bilateral nasal cavity, slightly enlarged inferior turbinates, hypertrophic middle turbinates, and a small amount of purulent nasal discharge in both middle nasal passages and posterior nostrils. Complete blood count, electrolyte profiles, and liver function were normal. A computed tomography scan from another hospital showed bilateral maxillary sinusitis, ethmoiditis, and bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy. A preoperative noncontrast chest computed tomography scan revealed a high-riding, tortuous structure extending to the mid-upper level of the first thoracic vertebra with local cystic dilatation, and a fe. Confirmed diagnosis: Cervical aortic arch with aneurysm formation and an anomalous right subclavian artery and left vertebral artery. Differential diagnosis includes: Cervical aortic arch with aneurysm formation and an anomalous right subclavian artery and left vertebral artery.

Asthma diagnosis is often suspected when a constellation of typical features is present, however, as most guidelines highlight, diagnosis has to be confirmed either by objective tests or an objective response to treatment. One of the initial major error that occurs is that insufficient features of the asthma pattern are sought before the diagnosis is made. knowledge_chunks.text: Both adult and child migraineurs are frequently misdiagnosed as having “sinus headaches”. In one adult study, 35% of the migraineurs had undergone previous sinus surgery. This was demonstrated by an observational study that included 3000 individuals with a history of self- or clinician-diagnosed “sinus headaches”, in which 88% of these patients met the diagnostic criteria for migraine. However, most of these patients reported additional typical migraine symptoms, such as photophobia, phonophobia, and pulsating head pain. Migraine can be mistaken for sinus headache because of the similarity in location of the headache and the commonly accompanying nasal autonomic symptoms. Pain due to pathology of the nasal mucosa or related structures is usually perceived as frontal or facial, but may be referred more posteriorly, making a proper diagnosis difficult. The presence of purulent nasal discharge and the character of the pain, which is typically pressure-like and reproduced by palpation over the sinuses, help to differentiate these two conditions.

A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents for worsening symptoms of previously diagnosed acute sinusitis. Initially, the pediatrician prescribed decongestants and sent the patient home. Since then, the patient has developed a nasal discharge with worsening pain. The patient has a medical history of asthma which is well-controlled with albuterol. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 90/48 mmHg, pulse is 124/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. Inspection of the patient's nose reveals a unilateral purulent discharge mixed with blood. The rest of the patient's exam is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Bleeding and infected vessel of Kiesselbach plexus
B. Foreign body obstruction
C. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
D. Septal perforation
E. Sinusitis with bacterial superinfection

knowledge_chunks.text: Both adult and child migraineurs are frequently misdiagnosed as having “sinus headaches”. In one adult study, 35% of the migraineurs had undergone previous sinus surgery. This was demonstrated by an observational study that included 3000 individuals with a history of self- or clinician-diagnosed “sinus headaches”, in which 88% of these patients met the diagnostic criteria for migraine. However, most of these patients reported additional typical migraine symptoms, such as photophobia, phonophobia, and pulsating head pain. Migraine can be mistaken for sinus headache because of the similarity in location of the headache and the commonly accompanying nasal autonomic symptoms. Pain due to pathology of the nasal mucosa or related structures is usually perceived as frontal or facial, but may be referred more posteriorly, making a proper diagnosis difficult. The presence of purulent nasal discharge and the character of the pain, which is typically pressure-like and reproduced by palpation over the sinuses, help to differentiate these two conditions.

As respiratory pediatricians we all experienced that low-dose inhaled corticosteroids can easily control asthma symptoms in most of patients. Moreover, exacerbations in children are often concentrated in some periods of the year due to viral trigger or aeroallergens, and some little patients can even stop their treatment in summer time without clinical deterioration. Nevertheless, children and their parents sometimes keep complaining of recurrent respiratory symptoms despite the correct and continuous treatment, and various courses of antibiotics, beta-2 agonists and oral corticosteroids are frequently prescribed by pediatrician. As a consequence of the poor symptoms control, asthma treatment is often increased and the patient categorized as “problematic severe asthmatic.” However, an earlier step could be identified and this condition better defined as “problematic respiratory symptoms unresponsive to prescribed asthma therapy”. In fact, the known expression: “Not all that wheezes is asthma” continues to be relevant and the asthma diagnosis should be clinically reconsidered. In the last few decades, we possibly moved from under diagnosing to over diagnosing asthma. Nowadays, a thriving child with history of recurrent cough and a need of frequent beta-2 and inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) treatment is often diagnosed with “probable asthma” and ICS in ever increasing doses immediately prescribed.
